prompt.context: Your client is looking at investing a significant amount of money to create an online auction company that facilitates sheep sales from producers to large customers. They will only do this if they could make roughly $10M annual profit in 5 years, and they have enlisted your help in determining the go/no-go decision.
prompt.question: Should the client invest in the online sheep auction company? Determine whether the venture can achieve $10M in annual profit within 5 years.

clarifying_info.q: What channels does sheep currently trade through?
clarifying_info.a: Sheep are sold either via auction or via direct contract. Sales via auction and contract will not migrate — there is no steal share between channels.
No. The percentage of farmers ('producers') who are online varies and grows over time — a chart is available showing the trend.

clarifying_info.q: What data is available to size the market?
clarifying_info.a: There are slides showing: overall market size in lbs of sheep, sheep prices in $/lb, farmers who use computers, and sheep sold at auction vs. contract.

exhibits.title: Annual Sheep Sales
exhibits.shows: Bar chart displaying annual sheep sales volume (in millions of lbs) from 2005 through 2010 (with 2006-2010 marked as expected/projected).
exhibits.data: Y-axis: 0 to 450 million lbs; values grow over the period; 2009/2010 values approach ~400 million lbs

exhibits.title: Auction Profitability by Channel
exhibits.shows: Stacked or grouped bar chart comparing the Online Auction Model vs. Traditional Auction Model. Each bar is broken into Sales Price per 100 lbs, Cost of Sales, and Profits.
exhibits.data: X-axis scale: $0 to $30 per 100 lbs; two channels shown: Online Auction Model and Traditional Auction Model; bars decomposed into Cost of Sales and Profits segments

exhibits.title: Sheep Sales by Channel
exhibits.shows: Bar chart showing the percentage split of total sheep sales between Auction and Contract channels.
exhibits.data: Y-axis: 0% to 100%; two segments per bar: Auction and Contract; auction appears to represent roughly 50% of sales

exhibits.title: Farmers Online
exhibits.shows: Line chart showing the percentage of sheep farmers ('producers') who are online, from 2005 through 2010 (with future years projected).
exhibits.data: Y-axis: 0% to 50%; values grow year over year; by 2009 the figure is approximately 30%

framework: Market sizing: estimate total lbs of sheep sold annually (use 2009 as the 5-year maturity year)
Channel split: determine what share of sheep sales flow through auctions (vs. direct contract)
Online penetration: determine what share of farmers (producers) are online and can use the platform
Revenue/profit per unit: read the profit per 100 lbs that the online auction model earns
Calculate total profit: multiply lbs × auction share × online farmer share × profit per 100 lbs
Compare to $10M hurdle and advise on go/no-go
Identify levers to close the gap if the base case falls short

questions.prompt: Using the exhibits, calculate the maximum annual profit the online auction platform can earn at 5-year maturity (use 2009 numbers).
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the four key inputs from the exhibits, multiply them together, and compare to the $10M target. Strong candidates note that penetration within the addressable auction market is implicitly 100% in this model (all online farmers participating) and that no channel migration is assumed.

math.setup: Profit = (Total sheep lbs) × (% sold at auction) × (% farmers online) × (profit per 100 lbs ÷ 100)
steps: Total sheep lbs in 2009: ~400 million lbs
Share sold at auction: 50% → 400M × 50% = 200M lbs auctioned
Share of farmers who are online in 2009: 30% → 200M × 30% = 60M lbs addressable
Profit per 100 lbs on online auction model: $10 → 60M lbs × ($10 / 100 lbs) = $6M
Note: the casebook states the answer as $6.66M, implying slightly different readings off the charts (e.g., 33% online farmers or ~400M lbs slightly higher). Acceptable range is ~$6–7M.
math.answer: ~$6.66M in annual profit — well short of the $10M target

questions.prompt: The profit calculation comes in far below $10M. What would you recommend the client do to reach the $10M profit level?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm levers across supply (more farmers online), demand (more volume through auction), pricing/margin (improve profit per 100 lbs), and scope expansion (other animals or geographies). Strong answers are structured and prioritized.

questions.prompt: If the product were already launched, how would you choose to market it?
questions.guidance: Candidate should think about reaching farmers (supply side) and processors (demand side), and consider both push and pull strategies. Strong answers include channel-specific ideas and a value proposition.

brainstorming.prompt: What would you do to reach the $10M profit level from the current projected ~$6.66M?

categories.name: Increase online farmer adoption
ideas: Train farmers and sheep producers on computer use
Provide central computer locations near farm sites to facilitate farmer interactions
Subsidize hardware or internet access for rural producers

categories.name: Expand scope
ideas: Expand the auction tool to other animals (cattle, goats, hogs)
Extend to additional geographies or international markets

categories.name: Marketing and go-to-market
ideas: Trade magazine advertisements targeting agricultural producers
Commissioned farmer representatives who earn fees on transactions
Build relationships with large sheep processors to create pull-driven demand

categories.name: Value proposition / pricing
ideas: Emphasize cost savings in moving herd to physical auction site — producers can have buyers pick up the herd at the farm
Improve platform margin by reducing cost of sales
Increase transaction fee per 100 lbs if market supports it

recommendation: Base case projects ~$6.66M annual profit at 5-year maturity, which is below the $10M threshold — the investment does not meet the client's hurdle rate as currently modeled.
A go decision would require meaningful upside from one or more levers: materially higher online farmer adoption, scope expansion to other livestock, or improved unit economics.
risks: Online farmer adoption may grow more slowly than projected in rural areas
Large processors already use computers but may resist switching from established contract relationships
No channel migration assumed — if true, addressable market is structurally capped
Competitive entry could compress the $10/100 lbs profit margin
next_steps: Validate online-farmer adoption curve with more granular survey data
Model sensitivity: what adoption rate or margin improvement gets to $10M?
Assess feasibility and incremental revenue from expanding to other animal categories
Design a pilot to test farmer uptake and willingness to pay before full investment
